The highest-transfer analogue (0.8157) shows only 24% brain penetration relative to plasma in rat, making it the strongest individual anchor because it combines the highest transfer score with a direct systemic brain-penetration measurement. Its structure contains an ionizable piperidine and several polar functionalities but is not an obvious extreme BBB non-penetrant. The experimental result therefore outweighs any more favorable physicochemical intuition: whatever mechanism limits its CNS exposure is real. claims.claim: Cefamandole, the closest analogue sharing the cephem/tetrazolethiomethyl core, showed only 2.5% CSF penetration in a rabbit pneumococcal meningitis model and was described as relatively poor, directly demonstrating that this chemotype can have inadequate CNS access even with inflammation.

In children with bacterial meningitis, cefamandole CSF levels were 10-40% of simultaneous serum levels, showing that the same close analogue can achieve meaningful CNS exposure when the BBB is inflamed.
Cefoperazone, another close analogue with p-hydroxyphenyl and tetrazolethio substituents, was capable of penetrating the BBB with a brain/blood AUC ratio of about 7.8% in rats.
Cefoxitin, a 7-methoxy cephamycin, reached CSF concentrations about 30% of simultaneous blood levels in a patient with meningitis, indicating that cephamycins can penetrate inflamed meninges.

Cephalothin produced low or unmeasurable brain tissue levels after intravenous infusion in humans, showing that some cephalosporins fail to achieve meaningful CNS access despite systemic administration.
Cefpodoxime showed low CSF penetration of approximately 5% in a piglet model, supporting limited CNS access for highly polar cephalosporins.

content.decision_summary: Cefotetan is a highly polar, dianionic cephamycin with an extra carboxylate and a 7-methoxy group. The closest analogues show only poor-to-modest CSF/brain penetration (cefamandole 2.5% in rabbit; cefoperazone 7.8% brain/blood AUC), and more polar cephalosporins such as cephalothin and cefpodoxime fail to achieve meaningful CNS access. Although some cephalosporins penetrate inflamed meninges, cefotetan's additional charge and polarity make adequate CNS access unlikely.
evidence_gaps: No direct cefotetan CSF or brain penetration data are available in the provided evidence.
Most supportive penetration data come from inflamed meninges; normal BBB penetration is likely lower.
Transporter-mediated efflux of cefotetan at the BBB is not directly quantified.
